sections.html:
In south-central New Mexico, on the Texas border, Otero County has one city: Alamogordo, the county seat. Cloudcroft and Tularosa are villages. Smaller places include Boles Acres, High Rolls, La Luz, Mayhill, Mescalero, Orogrande, Timberon and Holloman AFB. The 2020 census counted 67,839 people.

Holloman Air Force Base employs the most people, with tourism around Cloudcroft, the Mescalero resort and White Sands National Park next. Some owners arrive for a fixed tour at the base and must leave on a set date, which leaves little room to handle repairs, a tax bill or a listing.

Property tax runs through two county offices at the same Alamogordo address. Finding, listing and valuing property is the Assessor's task, while the Treasurer sends out the bill and receives payment. Take a disputed value to the Assessor, and a payoff question to the Treasurer.

OfficeWhat it doesAddress and phone
Otero County AssessorSets values, mails the notice of value, hears protests1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Alamogordo, NM 88310; 575-437-5310
Otero County TreasurerSends bills and accepts payment1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310; 575-437-2030
NM Property Tax DivisionHolds auctions for long-delinquent propertySanta Fe; 505-827-0883

Each county office has searchable online records. The Treasurer's EagleWeb portal displays balances, and the Assessor's portal displays current ownership.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
Otero County splits the year into two installments. The first half is payable by November 10 and late once December 10 passes. April 10 is the second-half deadline, late after May 10.

The Treasurer's office accepts payment at the counter, by mail, over the web or on the phone. The county's pay-by-phone page gives 1-877-707-1126, or 575-437-2030 and option 2. Credit cards run 2.39 percent with a $1.95 floor, while debit cards run $3.95.

  • November 10: pay the first installment
  • December 10: last penalty-free day for it
  • April 10: pay the second installment
  • May 10: last penalty-free day for that one

Owing does not depend on receiving. If the mail never brings your bill, the tax is still due, so tell the Assessor whenever your address changes.

The Assessor sets the value, and contesting it has a 30-day clock. Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978 sends the petition to the county assessor, due on April 1 or thirty days after the valuation notice is mailed, whichever comes later. It names the owner and property, explains the error and gives the figure you think is right.

A valuation protests board of three voting members hears each case and must rule within 180 days of filing. If you disagree with its ruling, district court is open to you for thirty days after the order.

There is also a ceiling on taxable home values. Under Section 7-36-21.2, a residential value cannot pass the greater of 103 percent of last year's figure or 106.1 percent of the figure from two years ago. The ceiling does not cover first-year valuations, last year's improvements, or the year after a sale or rezoning.

The sale exception is the one to remember. A buyer may see a higher assessed value the year after closing, so your old bill will not tell you what the new owner pays.

Penalty and interest come first, and after enough years a state auction can follow. The Property Tax Division runs these sales, not the county. Bidding starts at taxes, penalty, interest and costs, and a sale is held only after title research is done and other collection steps are used up. Not every one of the 33 counties has an auction each year.

Only the tax lien is wiped out by a tax sale. Other liens survive. What the buyer receives is a tax deed, which acts like a quitclaim and carries no title warranty. Former owners cannot redeem in New Mexico, but Section 7-38-70 allows a two-year court challenge.

With several years of tax behind on an Otero County house, move early. A sale before the property lands on an auction list leaves the equity in your hands.

Three things matter most: a current payoff, a clean record of ownership and a plan for both installments. The Treasurer supplies the balance, and the title or escrow company wants it before closing.

  • Look up the balance on the Treasurer's portal and confirm each half of this year.
  • Scan for older years too. Long-delinquent tax is what pushes a property toward auction.
  • Check the mailing address on the tax roll. Both the notice of value and the bill are sent there.
  • With a mobile home, ask the Assessor about a tax release before you try to move the title.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in this position, among them heirs of a house with tax behind it and owners who moved away. We buy as-is, so a stale tax bill, a half-done repair or a tenant need not be sorted out beforehand. Before you talk to any buyer, collect your deed, the newest bill and the Treasurer's payoff, so every offer can be weighed against what you truly owe.

sections.h2: A seller's order of work in Otero County
sections.html:
Military postings, inheritances and moves out of state all put owners under time pressure. Working in the right order keeps a short timeline from turning into a mistake.

  1. Start in the Assessor's portal and make sure the owner of record and the property description are correct. Errors here slow every later step.
  2. Open the Treasurer's portal, or call 575-437-2030, and note what is owed for each year.
  3. Look at your Notice of Value. If the number seems high and the protest window is still open, an informal talk with the Assessor costs nothing.
  4. Send the payoff to the title or escrow office, which will pay the Treasurer out of your closing money.
  5. Give the buyer a forwarding address for any bill that lands after the sale, and tell the Assessor too.

If you must be gone by a certain date, mention it at the start. Cash buyers can often adapt to a tight schedule, while a financed sale depends on an appraisal and lender review that you do not control. Either way, keep copies of every notice from the Assessor and the Treasurer in one folder, because the title company may ask for any of them on short notice.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Otero County property tax?
faqs.a: Go to the Otero County Treasurer at 1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310, or call 575-437-2030. Online and phone payments are also accepted, the phone number being 1-877-707-1126.

faqs.q: When is the first half of Otero County property tax due?
faqs.a: November 10 is the first-half due date, with delinquency after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and goes delinquent after May 10.

faqs.q: How long do I have to protest my Otero County valuation?
faqs.a: Whichever comes later, April 1 or thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. Send the Otero County Assessor a petition giving your reason and your figure.

faqs.q: Can the county sell my house at auction for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: Only the state auctions property after long delinquency. Sales by the Property Tax Division are as is, at a floor of the taxes, penalty, interest and costs, with no right of redemption.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Otero County house that has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company asks the Treasurer for a payoff, and the balance is taken from your proceeds at closing. Selling before the auction list avoids that outcome.
